judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 1222, the Maryland Values Act, which limited where federal immigration agents can go in the state. Public schools, public libraries, and state and local government offices must keep those agents out of the parts of their buildings that are closed to the public. Agents may still enter with a warrant signed by a judge, or in an emergency. Jails and courthouse lockups are not covered. A federal officer must also notify certain people before acting at one of these places. The Attorney General had to publish guidance, and each covered school, library, and office had to adopt a matching policy by October 1, 2025. By July 1, 2026 each must also publish steps that stop personal records and location data from being sold or shared in ways that hurt residents' privacy. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 101-38 and it was signed into law as Chapter 718 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 1424, the Protect Our Federal Workers Act, which offered state help to Marylanders who lost federal jobs. It let two state emergency funds be spent on former federal workers, and renamed one of them the Federal Government Employee Assistance Loan Fund. It changed who may borrow from that fund and allowed some loans to be forgiven, meaning the money never has to be paid back. It moved $5.0 million into that fund in fiscal 2025 from the Rainy Day Fund, the state's savings account. It gave the Attorney General more power to go to court over federal actions that harm Marylanders, and required at least $2.5 million a year for that office. It also set up a temporary program to hire people who left federal service into open state jobs. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 105-33 and it was signed into law as Chapter 97 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 424, the Lowering Prescription Drug Costs for All Marylanders Now Act, which gave the state's Prescription Drug Affordability Board more power over high drug prices. The board sets upper payment limits, which are caps on what can be paid for a drug. The bill dropped some of the board's reporting duties. Instead the board must decide whether caps are in the state's best interest for drugs that cost people too much, and set them if it decides they are. It may set those caps for drugs bought or paid for by state and local government. It may not use a cap against Medicare Advantage or Medicare drug plan payment rules, count a pharmacy's dispensing fee toward a cap, or put a new cap on a drug that is in short supply. The bill added members to the board's advisory council. Widening the caps to cover all buyers and insurers depends on other steps happening by September 30, 2030. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 100-38 and it was signed into law as Chapter 611 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass SB 901, which made the companies that produce packaging and paper products responsible for recycling what they sell. Each producer must send a recycling plan to the Maryland Department of the Environment for approval by July 1, 2028. After a date the department sets, a producer may not sell or ship covered packaging in Maryland without an approved plan. The department must list which materials are covered, keep studying what the state's recycling system needs, and enforce the rules. The bill also changed the state's existing advisory council on the subject and set rules for the companies hired to do the work. The Maryland Senate passed it 33-11 and it was signed into law as Chapter 431 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass SB 848, which created the Public Health Abortion Grant Program to help people get abortion care. The money comes from leftover funds in the separate accounts that health insurers must keep for abortion care under the federal Affordable Care Act. The Insurance Commissioner must order that money moved into a new state fund. The Governor had to put $2.0 million of it toward the program by October 1, 2025. Starting in fiscal 2027 the Governor must budget at least 90% of the leftover money for the fund each year. The Maryland Senate passed it 29-15 and it was signed into law as Chapter 436 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 1378, which cut how much money child sexual abuse victims can win in cases Maryland had recently reopened. Those cases had been blocked by filing deadlines until the state lifted them. The bill lowered the limits on what victims can collect from the state, from local governments, and from local school boards. It also lowered the cap on damages for pain and suffering in other reopened cases. It changed those limits so they apply once per claim instead of once per incident. It also capped the fees a victim's lawyer may charge. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 91-41 and it was signed into law as Chapter 104 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 39, the Carlton R. Smith Act, which erased Maryland's crime of passing on HIV. Knowingly giving or trying to give someone HIV had been a misdemeanor, the lower level of crime. The bill removed it and its penalty. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 100-36 and it was signed into law as Chapter 651 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 983, which set up help for voters who do not speak English well. The State Board of Elections must decide which counties have a real need for help in another language. Local election boards in those counties must provide it, including a way for a voter to reach a translator and talk with election judges at an early voting center or a polling place. The state board had to post the list of covered local boards on its website by January 1, 2026. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 97-30 and it was signed into law as Chapter 278 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 1020, the Fair Medical Debt Reporting Act, which kept medical debt off credit reports. Credit reporting companies may not list covered medical debt, and no one may use it to decide whether a person is good for a loan. Doctors, hospitals, and sellers of medical products may not report any part of a medical debt to those companies. They must also put that ban in writing in any contract that sells or hands off medical debt for collection. A contract signed after the law took effect without that promise cannot be enforced. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 102-37 and it was signed into law as Chapter 121 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 197, which told the state to plan for restorative practices schools. Restorative practices is a discipline model that repairs relationships instead of punishing. By July 1, 2026 the Maryland State Department of Education must write a full plan for setting these up, using outside experts, and must help schools that ask. A local school board that opens one must follow it. The department must report to the Governor and the General Assembly by December 1, 2026. The state's school discipline rules now say restorative practices instead of approaches. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 94-36 and it was signed into law as Chapter 240 of 2025.
